name: Thu Lao
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.quote: The Bu Dai language is fundamentally, as the other Tai dialects, a monosyllabic tonal language, the syllabic structure of which is C1V(C2)/T (where the appearance of C2 is not obligatory). C1 is the initial consonant, V is the vocalic nucleus and C2 is the final consonant. T is a supra-segmental feature — the tone. [fn. 3:] Strictly speaking, there is an occasional so-called 'minor syllable' attached in front of this fundamental word structure. In terms of stress, it is always weaker than that of the following major syllable and its segmental realization varies slightly according to the vowel in the major syllable. Tonally, there seems to be a difference at least between 'high' and 'middle'. [...] In this article, we focused on major syllables and abstained from making a concrete analysis of minor syllables.
new_statements.citation: Kosaka, Ryuichi. 1997. A Phonology of the Bu Dai (Thu Lao) Language. Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies) 53: 137-153.
new_statements.locator: p. 139, sect. 1.1 'Initials' first paragraph + footnote 3 (stress statement); p. 143, sect. 1.4 'Tones' (five tones)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Monosyllabic lexical-tone language with five tones on the major syllable (p. 143: 1 mid-high falling, 2 low level, 3 high level, 4 mid level, 5 mid-low rising); no word-stress rule is stated. The only stress statement is that an occasional prefixed 'minor syllable' (e.g. /kə-/, /hə-/, /pə-/, /lə-/, /mi-/ in animal names) is always weaker in stress than the following major syllable, i.e. prominence sits on the tone-bearing final major syllable of a sesquisyllabic word.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Kosaka explicitly abstains from analysing minor syllables, so the minor-syllable tone contrast ('high' vs 'middle') is left open.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the statement concerns a minor syllable 'attached in front of this fundamental word structure'; elicited citation forms from a single informant (Mrs Vang Diu Sinh, 23, Na Cang hamlet, Xin Ma Cai, Bac Ha, Lao Cai, via a Nung-language questionnaire, 1996). Nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: thul1247 is a Glottolog 5.3 'Bookkeeping' (retired) entry: 'The Thu Lao [tyl] entry E16-E28 represents the same language as the Dai Zhuang entry [zhd] (Kosaka 1997) but spoken in Vietnam. See also: Dai Zhuang [zhd].' ISO 639-3 still lists tyl as Active (Wikipedia: 'tyl - Thu Lao (duplicate code)'); zhd was created by change request 2006-128 (split of ccy Southern Zhuang), whose request file names 'Thu Lao' as the Vietnamese exonym (200 speakers, Muong Khuong District, Lao Cai). The language is ALREADY in our catalog as daiz1235 'Bu Dai (Thu Lao) (Glottolog: Dai Zhuang)', deciding source Kosaka 1997 (classification tonal-OR-pitch accent, A+B confirmed 2026-09-12, re-checked 2026-09-16/17). Kosaka's own informant lect is the Bu Dai of Na Cang hamlet, Xin Ma Cai village, Bac Ha district, Lao Cai (p. 138); he equates it with Zhang Junru's Thu Lao = Wenma patois of Zhuang (Wenshan, Yunnan) and with the Thu Lao of Ngo Duc Thinh & Chu Thai Son 1975. by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) thul1247 should be merged into daiz1235, not given its own row.
